stem: A chat application sends only the newest user message to the Messages endpoint on each turn. Users report that Claude has no awareness of anything said earlier in the same conversation. What explains this behavior, and what is the correct remedy?

options.text: Conversation state is retained on the server for a limited period, and these requests are arriving after that period has lapsed.
The Messages API is stateless, so the client must resend the full conversation history in the messages array on every request.
The id returned on a response acts as a conversation handle, and resending it on the next request restores the earlier turns.
History is retained only when a request enables incremental delivery, so the application needs to turn on streaming responses.

explanation: The Messages API is stateless. It keeps no conversation state between calls, so the model can only reference what is present in the request it receives. To build a multi-turn conversation, the client accumulates the prior user and assistant turns and resends the whole messages array each time. A useful corollary is that earlier assistant turns need not be verbatim reproductions of what Claude actually returned; synthetic assistant messages are legal and are a documented technique for steering a conversation. Because the client owns the transcript, it also owns the cost and context consequences of letting that transcript grow unchecked.

distractorNotes.a: There is no server-side conversation store to expire. Prompt caching can make a repeated prefix cheaper to process, but it caches computation rather than conversation state and never supplies history the client did not send.
distractorNotes.c: The id on a response identifies that one message. It is not a conversation handle, and resending it does not cause the API to rehydrate any earlier turns.
distractorNotes.d: Streaming changes only how a single response is delivered over the wire. It has no bearing on whether conversation history is retained between requests.

sourceNote: Using the Messages API - 'Multiple conversational turns' section, which states the API is stateless and the full conversational history must be sent on each request

stem: A developer is reviewing how the Messages API interprets the body of a create-message request. Which statements are correct? Select THREE.

options.text: A request is rejected outright unless the user and assistant roles strictly alternate through the array with no repetition of the same role.
Two adjacent messages that carry the same role are combined into a single turn rather than rejected.
A message whose content is a plain string is equivalent to that same content expressed as a single text content block.
max_tokens acts as a target length, so responses will land close to the value supplied.
max_tokens sets an upper bound on generation, and a response may stop on its own before reaching that bound.
When a system prompt is supplied, the messages array must begin with an assistant message.

explanation: Three behaviors matter when constructing a request body. First, the models are trained on alternating user and assistant turns, but consecutive same-role messages are merged into one turn rather than raising an error, which means a client bug that appends two user messages fails silently rather than loudly. Second, a string value for content is shorthand for an array holding one text block, so the two forms are interchangeable and a client can move to the block form whenever it needs images, documents, or cache controls. Third, max_tokens is a ceiling on generation and nothing more; the model routinely finishes earlier, which is why stop_reason exists to tell you which of the two occurred.

distractorNotes.a: Strict alternation is not enforced. Consecutive same-role turns are merged into a single turn, which is precisely why this class of client bug is easy to miss.
distractorNotes.d: max_tokens is an absolute maximum, not a target. The model may and often does stop before reaching it, which is reported as a stop_reason of end_turn rather than max_tokens.
distractorNotes.f: No such requirement exists. The system prompt is supplied through its own top-level field and does not constrain which role opens the messages array.

sourceNote: Messages API reference - 'Body parameters' entries for messages and max_tokens, covering turn merging, string-versus-block content equivalence, and the max_tokens ceiling

stem: To force a particular output shape, an integration ends its messages array with an assistant message containing a partial sentence. Against a model that does not support assistant-message prefill, the request fails. What does the API return, and what is the documented alternative?

options.text: A 200 response carrying a refusal stop reason, which the client should handle by retrying the same call against a designated fallback model.
A 422 unprocessable_entity, resolved by relocating the partial text into the top-level system field so it is read as an instruction.
A 400 invalid_request_error saying the conversation must end with a user message; use structured outputs or system prompt instructions instead.
A 429 rate_limit_error, because text supplied in a prefilled assistant turn is charged against the output token allowance for the request.

explanation: Prefilling the assistant turn was a long-standing steering technique, but on models that do not support it the request is rejected at validation time with a 400 invalid_request_error whose message states that the conversation must end with a user message. This is a validation failure rather than a runtime or capacity condition, so no retry strategy will help. The documented replacements are structured outputs, which constrain the response to a supplied schema through constrained decoding, or ordinary system prompt instructions describing the desired format. Because prefill support varies across the lineup, an integration that depends on it should treat that dependency as a portability risk and confirm support before changing models.

distractorNotes.a: A refusal stop reason describes a model declining to answer a request that was accepted. Here the request never reaches generation, because it is rejected during validation.
distractorNotes.b: 422 is not among the status codes this API returns. Moving prefill text into the system field also changes its meaning, since system content is an instruction rather than the opening of the assistant's reply.
distractorNotes.d: 429 signals a rate or spend condition. An unsupported request shape has nothing to do with throughput, and no amount of backoff will make the request succeed.

sourceNote: Claude API errors - 'Common validation errors' subsection 'Prefill not supported', giving the 400 invalid_request_error and the structured outputs alternative

stem: An application inspects stop_reason on every response to decide what to do next. Which mapping of a stop_reason value to the required follow-up action is correct?

options.text: pause_turn means the client should discard the assistant content produced so far and resend the original user message unchanged.
end_turn means the response was cut short partway through and the client should immediately request a continuation of it.
stop_sequence means one of the configured sequences fired nondeterministically, so the identical request should simply be retried until it completes normally.
tool_use means the client should run the requested client-side tool and return its output as a tool_result block in the next user message.

explanation: stop_reason is the control signal that drives an agent loop. A value of tool_use means the model has emitted a tool call and is waiting on the caller: the client runs the tool it defined and returns the outcome as a tool_result block in the following user message, keyed to the originating tool_use id. The other values each imply a distinct action. end_turn means the response is complete and usable. max_tokens means the client's own ceiling truncated the output. pause_turn means a server-side tool loop reached its iteration limit and the assistant content must be sent back so work can continue. refusal means the model declined, with accompanying detail identifying the policy category involved.

distractorNotes.a: A paused turn is resumed by sending the assistant content produced so far back to the API, not by discarding it. Throwing that content away loses completed work and restarts the loop from the beginning.
distractorNotes.b: end_turn is the ordinary completion signal and means the response should be used as-is. Truncation against a client-supplied ceiling is reported as max_tokens instead.
distractorNotes.c: This value means one of the caller's own configured stop sequences was emitted. The response reports which one fired, and reissuing the same request will simply reproduce it.

sourceNote: Stop reasons and fallback - 'Quick reference' table mapping each stop_reason value to its meaning and the recommended follow-up action

stem: A client consumes a streamed Messages response over server-sent events without using an official SDK helper. Which statements about correct handling of that stream are true? Select THREE.

options.text: Token counts reported on message_delta events are cumulative rather than per-event increments, so summing them across events overcounts usage.
Each content block delta carries a complete, independently parseable JSON object representing the block's accumulated input.
Deltas for a tool_use block arrive as partial JSON fragments that must be accumulated before they can be parsed as an object.
Receiving an unrecognized event type indicates a corrupted stream, so the connection should be torn down and the whole request retried from the beginning.
The terminating event repeats the full accumulated text, so clients do not need to accumulate text deltas themselves.
An error can be delivered inside the event stream after the HTTP response has already returned a success status.

explanation: Hand-rolled streaming clients get caught out in three predictable places. Usage counts on message_delta events are cumulative, so a client that adds them up as increments reports inflated token totals. Tool input arrives as partial JSON string fragments, and only the final assembled value is guaranteed to be a valid object, so parsing must wait until the block closes. And because the stream opens with a success status before generation finishes, a failure such as an overload condition can arrive as an error event mid-stream, which means status-code-based error handling alone is not sufficient. A fourth discipline follows from the versioning policy: unknown event types must be ignored gracefully, since new ones can be introduced without a version change.

distractorNotes.b: Tool input deltas are explicitly partial JSON strings rather than standalone objects. Attempting to parse an individual fragment will usually fail on incomplete syntax.
distractorNotes.d: New event types may be added over time, so an unrecognized type is an expected condition. Tearing down the connection turns a forward-compatible stream into a self-inflicted outage.
distractorNotes.e: The terminating event closes the stream; it does not restate the generated content. A client that discards deltas as they arrive ends up with nothing to display.

sourceNote: Streaming messages - 'Event types', 'Error events', 'Other events', and 'Content block delta types' sections covering cumulative usage, mid-stream errors, and partial JSON input deltas

stem: An agent loop frequently receives a near-empty assistant response carrying a stop_reason of end_turn. Inspecting the transcript shows that each tool_result block is followed, inside the same user message, by an extra text block that summarizes what the tool returned. What is the documented cause?

options.text: Appending a text block after a tool_result leads the model to treat its own turn as already concluded, so it ends the turn early.
tool_result blocks belong in an assistant message, and placing them in a user message causes the turn to terminate prematurely.
The identifier linking the result to its originating tool call was omitted, so the API discards the result and the model has nothing to answer.
Near-empty responses of this shape always indicate that the model's available context window has been completely exhausted.

explanation: This is a documented and easily missed failure mode. When a client appends its own commentary text directly after a tool_result, the model learns from the pattern that the user always supplies text once results arrive, and it concludes its own turn accordingly, yielding a very short response with an ordinary end_turn stop reason. The fix is to return tool results on their own, with no additional text blocks in that message. A related instance of the same pattern occurs when a client sends Claude's already-completed response back unchanged: the model has already judged itself finished and will remain so. Note that this presents as a well-formed successful response rather than an error, which is why it usually surfaces as a quality complaint rather than an exception.

distractorNotes.b: tool_result blocks are correctly returned inside a user message. Moving them to an assistant message would misrepresent who produced the result and is not the cause described here.
distractorNotes.c: A missing tool identifier is a request validation problem and would surface as an error, not as a well-formed response carrying an end_turn stop reason.
distractorNotes.d: Exhausting the context window is reported through its own dedicated stop reason. An end_turn response reflects the model choosing to stop rather than the window running out.

sourceNote: Stop reasons and fallback - 'Empty responses with end_turn' accordion under the end_turn section, listing text blocks appended after tool results as a common cause

stem: A team is estimating whether a planned request will fit inside a model's context window. Which components have to be counted?

options.text: Only the user and assistant message text, since system prompts and tool definitions are billed but sit outside the window itself.
Only the input side, since generated output is bounded separately by max_tokens and does not occupy space in the window.
Only the most recent turn, since earlier turns are summarized and compacted automatically before the request is processed.
The system prompt, every message including tool results and documents, the tool definitions, and the tokens generated in reply.

explanation: The context window is the model's entire working memory for a request, and everything sent counts toward it: the system prompt, every entry in the messages array including tool results, images, and documents, and the tool definitions themselves. Critically, the output side counts too, because the window has to hold the response being generated alongside everything that prompted it. Tool definitions are the component teams most often forget, since they are configuration rather than conversation and can grow substantial once a toolset expands. The token counting endpoint exists to estimate a request before it is sent, and each response reports actual consumption in its usage field, which is the more reliable signal for capacity planning.

distractorNotes.a: System prompts and tool definitions are part of the request the model reads, so they occupy the window like any other input. Tool definitions in particular can dominate the budget in a tool-heavy agent.
distractorNotes.b: The window holds the response as well as the prompt. max_tokens caps how much may be generated, but that generated output still has to fit inside the same window.
distractorNotes.c: Server-side compaction is an explicitly enabled feature rather than default behavior. On an ordinary request, prior turns are present because the client resent them and they consume window space in full.

sourceNote: Context windows - 'How the context window works' section enumerating what counts toward the window, including system prompt, messages, tool definitions, and generated output

stem: A nightly job classifies a large backlog of documents. No result is consumed interactively, and cost is the dominant constraint. Which approach fits, and which design constraint must be accepted alongside it?

options.text: Use the Message Batches API but stream each result as it finishes, since entries within a batch support per-request incremental delivery.
Use synchronous requests with a long client timeout, since batch submission carries a price premium in exchange for its throughput.
Use the Message Batches API for asynchronous processing at reduced cost, accepting polling for results and no streaming inside a batch.
Use synchronous requests, since a batch accepts only single-turn text prompts and rejects tools, system prompts, and image inputs.

explanation: Bulk work with no interactive consumer is the canonical fit for the Message Batches API, which processes requests asynchronously at a substantial discount to synchronous pricing. The design trade-offs are real and must be planned for. Results are retrieved by polling rather than held on an open connection, which is itself an advantage for long jobs because it removes the risk of a dropped connection. Requests that do not complete inside the processing window expire and must be resubmitted, so the job needs to be idempotent and re-runnable. Streaming is unavailable within a batch, since results are returned as a single file rather than incrementally. Almost everything else carries over, including tools, system prompts, multi-turn conversations, and vision.

distractorNotes.a: Streaming is explicitly unsupported inside a batch, because results are returned as a file once processing ends rather than incrementally over a live connection.
distractorNotes.b: Batch processing is cheaper than synchronous processing, not more expensive. Holding a synchronous connection open across a bulk job also exposes it to idle-connection failures.
distractorNotes.d: Batches accept essentially the full range of Messages requests, including tools, system prompts, multi-turn conversations, and vision, and different request types can be mixed within one batch.

sourceNote: Batch processing - 'How the Message Batches API works', 'Batch limitations', and 'What can be batched' sections, including the table of parameters unsupported in batch requests

stem: A team is introducing prompt caching into a service that reuses a large block of shared instructions across many requests. Which statements about how caching behaves are correct? Select THREE.

options.text: Cache markers may only be placed on system content, so message content cannot take part in a cached prefix at all.
A cache entry covers the prefix in the order tools, then system, then messages, up to the block that carries the cache marker.
A cache hit requires the entire request to match exactly, including the newest user message, or the existing entry is discarded and written again.
Reusing a cached prefix refreshes that entry's lifetime again, at no additional cost beyond the ordinary cache hit price.
Cached prefixes persist indefinitely until they are removed through a dedicated cache management endpoint.
An entry's lifetime is measured from the start of the request that reads or writes it, not from the point its response ends.

explanation: Three properties determine whether caching actually pays off. Caching operates on a prefix assembled in a fixed order, tools then system then messages, up to the marked block, which is why stable content must be placed early and volatile content late; a single reordering upstream invalidates everything after it. Reuse refreshes an entry's lifetime for free, so steady traffic against a shared prefix keeps it warm without extra charges. The timing subtlety catches teams out: the lifetime clock starts when the request begins, not when its response completes, so a long generation eats into the window available to the follow-up request that hoped to reuse the entry. Design accordingly by keeping the reusable prefix stable and appending anything that changes.

distractorNotes.a: Cache markers are placed on content blocks generally, and the cached prefix spans tools, system, and messages. Restricting caching to system content would exclude the growing conversation history that benefits most.
distractorNotes.c: Caching matches a prefix, not the whole request. Requiring an exact whole-request match would make caching useless, since the newest user message differs on every call.
distractorNotes.e: Entries are ephemeral and expire on a time-to-live basis. There is no deletion endpoint to call, and none is needed.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'How prompt caching works' section, including the note that caching covers tools, system, and messages in that order, and the explanation that the lifetime is measured from the start of the request

stem: An API-driven agent recalls details from its transcript less and less reliably as a session runs on, even though the transcript remains comfortably inside the model's context window. What does the guidance identify as the underlying issue and the appropriate response?

options.text: Accuracy and recall degrade as the token count grows, so context must be actively curated rather than simply allowed to accumulate.
The API applies the window on a first-in, first-out basis, so the earliest turns were silently evicted and now need to be re-sent.
Recall degrades only when tool definitions are present in the request, so pruning the unused tools from the toolset restores it.
The model's training cutoff limits how well it can recall material supplied in context, and no context management technique mitigates it.

explanation: Remaining under the limit is not the same as performing well. As the token count climbs, accuracy and recall degrade, an effect the documentation names context rot. The practical consequence is that a larger window is not automatically better and cannot substitute for context management: curating what occupies the window matters as much as how much room is left. This reframes context as a resource to be managed deliberately, through techniques such as server-side compaction for long-running sessions and through reducing the footprint of tool definitions, rather than as a budget to be filled until full. Trimming unused tools does help, but only as one instance of the broader curation principle.

distractorNotes.b: API requests do not evict turns implicitly. The client controls the transcript entirely, and rolling first-in, first-out behavior is a property of some chat interfaces rather than the API.
distractorNotes.c: Tool definitions consume window space and trimming them helps, but they are not the sole cause. Degradation tracks the total token count regardless of what those tokens contain.
distractorNotes.d: The training cutoff bounds what the model knows independently of the request. It does not govern how well the model uses material placed in its context.

sourceNote: Context windows - 'How the context window works' section describing context rot, that more context is not automatically better, and that curating context matters as much as available space

stem: A service calls the Messages endpoint over plain HTTP without using an official SDK. Which set of request headers must be present on every call?

options.text: The API key header and a content type header only, since the API version is negotiated between client and server automatically.
A credential header, either the API key header or an Authorization bearer token, plus the version header and a content type header.
The API key header, the version header, the content type header, and a workspace identifier header, regardless of how the key is scoped.
The version header and a beta feature header only, with the credential supplied as a query string parameter on the request URL.

explanation: Three headers are required on every direct HTTP request: a credential, which is either the API key header or an Authorization bearer token obtained through workload identity federation; the API version header; and a JSON content type header. The version header is the one most often overlooked, because the official SDKs set it automatically along with the other two, so the requirement becomes visible only when a team writes its own client or reproduces a call with a command-line tool. A workspace identifier header is conditional rather than universal: it is required when the key is permitted to act across multiple workspaces, and omitted when the key is already bound to a single workspace.

distractorNotes.a: The API version is never negotiated implicitly. Omitting the version header is a request error, and pinning a version is what makes the compatibility guarantees meaningful in the first place.
distractorNotes.c: The workspace identifier header is conditional rather than universal. A key scoped to one workspace already determines where the request runs, so sending the header there is unnecessary.
distractorNotes.d: Credentials travel in headers, never as query parameters, which would leak them into logs and referrer data. A beta header is needed only when a beta feature is actually being used.

sourceNote: API overview - 'Authentication' section header table listing which headers are required and noting that client SDKs send authentication, version, and content-type automatically

stem: An organization is replacing a personal API key that several engineers currently share to run a production service. Which approaches align with the documented guidance? Select TWO.

options.text: Have an administrator create a service account so the workload holds its own identity, and issue a key linked to that service account.
Create a workspace-scoped legacy key, since a credential that belongs to no individual is the recommended default for new integrations.
Keep the shared personal key but rotate it more often, since it already carries exactly the permissions the service needs.
Issue one personal key per engineer and have the service select one at random per request to spread usage across identities.
Federate the workload's existing platform identity so requests present short-lived tokens instead of a stored static secret.

explanation: A shared personal key acts as one specific person and stops working when that person leaves the organization, which makes it a production outage waiting on a personnel change. The guidance offers two sound replacements. A service account gives the workload its own managed identity, so the credential's lifetime is tied to the workload rather than to an employee. Workload identity federation goes further by removing the static secret entirely: the workload exchanges an identity token it already holds for a short-lived access token, which suits cloud platforms, CI pipelines, and container orchestrators where a platform identity already exists. Both grant the same access to the API endpoints, so the choice turns on whether the workload has a federatable identity available.

distractorNotes.b: Workspace-scoped keys still function but are explicitly legacy. Identity-backed keys or federation are preferred for new integrations, so this is the opposite of the recommended default.
distractorNotes.c: Rotation does not address the underlying defect. The key still acts as one individual and still breaks the moment that individual loses access to the organization.
distractorNotes.d: This multiplies the original problem rather than solving it, spreading production dependence across several personal identities that can each disappear independently.

sourceNote: Authentication - method comparison table and the 'Key types' section, which recommends service accounts for shared or automated workloads and marks workspace keys as legacy

stem: A team issues an API key that is permitted to act across several workspaces. Their service sends only the credential, version, and content type headers. What has to change so that requests run in the intended workspace?

options.text: Prefix the model identifier in the request body with the name of the workspace the call belongs to.
Nothing, because a multi-workspace key resolves the workspace from the model chosen in the request.
Recreate the credential as an administrative key, because only those keys can select a workspace.
Send the identifier of the target workspace in the workspace header on each request the service makes.

explanation: Workspace selection is header-driven. A key bound to one workspace carries that binding implicitly and may omit the header, which is why single-workspace keys are convenient for a service that only ever runs in one environment. A key permitted to act across several workspaces has no implicit target, so the workspace identifier header is required on each request to say where the call should run. This matters beyond routing, because workspaces are the boundary for rate limits, spend limits, and usage reporting, so an unscoped request lands the traffic in the wrong accounting bucket. Workspace identifiers can be read from the console workspace settings or listed through the administrative API.

distractorNotes.a: The model identifier names a model and nothing more. Workspace targeting is expressed through headers rather than encoded into request body values.
distractorNotes.b: Model choice and workspace are independent of one another. The same model can be called from any workspace the key can reach, so it cannot disambiguate the target.
distractorNotes.c: Administrative keys serve organization-level endpoints. Ordinary keys select a workspace through the header, and a workspace-scoped key is in fact rejected by the administrative endpoints.

sourceNote: Authentication - 'Select a workspace' section stating that keys not scoped to a workspace must specify the workspace ID header on each request

stem: A client library pins a specific API version value on every request. Under the documented version guarantees, which changes must that client tolerate without breaking? Select THREE.

options.text: New optional request parameters being introduced on endpoints the client already calls.
Removal of a response field the client currently reads, with no change to the pinned version value.
Renaming of existing request parameters between releases inside the same pinned version.
Additional fields appearing in response payloads the client already parses.
Previously unseen values turning up in enumerated outputs, such as new streaming event types.
Silent redefinition of what an existing field's values mean, with the field name left unchanged.

explanation: Pinning a version buys a specific and bounded guarantee: existing input parameters and existing output parameters are preserved. What it does not buy is a frozen surface. Additional optional inputs may appear, additional values may appear in outputs, and new variants may be added to enumerated outputs, streaming event types being the example the documentation calls out. The engineering consequence is that a client must parse defensively, ignoring unknown response fields rather than rejecting them, and handling unrecognized enumerated values gracefully rather than treating them as corruption. A strict parser that fails on anything unexpected will break on an additive change the version contract explicitly permits.

distractorNotes.b: Existing output parameters are preserved within a version. Field removal is precisely the kind of breaking change that pinning a version is meant to protect against.
distractorNotes.c: Existing input parameters are preserved within a version, so parameters are not renamed underneath a client that has pinned one.
distractorNotes.f: Redefining the meaning of existing values would break clients silently and is not among the permitted changes. The surface grows by adding new values, not by repurposing old ones.

sourceNote: Versions - opening section listing what is preserved for a given version and the permitted additive changes, including new variants in enum-like output values

stem: A production integration currently classifies failures by matching substrings of error messages and wraps every failure in its own fixed-interval retry loop. Which change aligns with the documented guidance?

options.text: Keep matching strings, but branch on the human-readable message text rather than on the error type raised by the SDK.
Catch the SDK's typed error classes, most specific first, and rely on its built-in backoff, which honors a retry-after header.
Retry every failure indefinitely with backoff, since each of the documented error types represents a transient condition.
Disable the SDK's retries and treat any non-success status as permanent, escalating at once instead of attempting recovery.

explanation: Two documented practices apply. First, the official SDKs raise typed exceptions rather than returning raw payloads, and the guidance is to catch those classes from most specific to least specific instead of string-matching messages, whose wording is free to change without breaking the version contract. Second, the SDKs already retry transient failures such as connection errors, rate limits, and server errors with exponential backoff, honoring a retry-after header when one is present, and the retry count is configurable per client. A bespoke fixed-interval loop layered on top duplicates that behavior, ignores the server's own guidance about when to retry, and can amplify load during an incident. Capturing the request identifier from each response completes the picture, since support investigations depend on it.

distractorNotes.a: Message wording is not part of the compatibility contract and may change at any time. Branching on it is the fragile practice the guidance advises replacing, not a refinement of it.
distractorNotes.c: Many failures are permanent, including authentication, permission, and validation errors. Retrying those indefinitely converts a clear failure into a silent hang and wastes quota.
distractorNotes.d: Some conditions genuinely are transient and are expected to be retried with backoff. Escalating all of them immediately discards recovery behavior the SDK already implements correctly.

sourceNote: Claude API errors - 'HTTP errors' paragraph on automatic SDK retries with exponential backoff and the 'SDK error types' section advising typed exception handling over string matching

stem: Which description of the documented model lifecycle states is correct?

options.text: A deprecated model stops serving requests at once, while a retired model continues to serve them at a reduced level of priority.
Legacy and retired describe a single state, differing only in whether a recommended replacement has already been published.
A deprecated model still serves requests and has a recommended replacement and a retirement date; a retired model fails requests.
A retired model continues to serve requests normally, but returns its responses without any accompanying usage accounting.

explanation: The lifecycle runs through four named states. Active means fully supported and recommended. Legacy means the model receives no further updates and may be deprecated later. Deprecated means still functional but no longer recommended, and it is the point at which a recommended replacement and a retirement date are published. Retired means unavailable, and requests to a retired model fail. The operationally important distinction is between deprecated and retired: deprecation is a warning with a deadline attached and is the window in which migration work belongs, whereas retirement is a hard cutoff. Deprecated models are also noted as likely to be less reliable than active ones, so lingering on one carries a cost even before the deadline arrives.

distractorNotes.a: This inverts the two states. Deprecation leaves a model serving traffic, and retirement is the point at which requests to it stop succeeding.
distractorNotes.b: Legacy and retired are distinct states. A legacy model still works but receives no further updates, whereas a retired model is no longer available at all.
distractorNotes.d: Retirement removes availability outright. There is no degraded serving mode in which a retired model still answers requests.

sourceNote: Model deprecations - 'Overview' section defining the active, legacy, deprecated, and retired lifecycle states

stem: A model that an application depends on has been announced for retirement. Which actions are supported by the documented migration guidance? Select THREE.

options.text: Assume the model will keep serving requests past the retirement date at reduced throughput, so the migration work can proceed at leisure after that date.
Export the organization's usage report from the console to find which API keys and models still call the affected model.
Re-run the application's evaluations against the recommended replacement well ahead of the retirement date.
Rely on the model identifier resolving automatically to the recommended replacement once the original has been retired.
Treat advance notice as unavailable for planning purposes, since retirements are announced without any notice period.
Verify the retirement schedule separately for any partner-operated cloud platform in use, because those platforms set their own dates.

explanation: Migration is a three-part exercise. Discovery comes first: the console usage export breaks consumption down by API key and model, which is how a team finds the forgotten job or stale service still pointing at the affected model. Validation comes next, since a replacement is not a drop-in equivalent and the guidance is explicit that applications should be tested against it well before the deadline, using the evaluation suite the team already maintains. Scope checking closes it out, because the published dates apply to platforms operated by Anthropic, while partner-operated cloud platforms publish their own schedules, so a multi-platform deployment can face several different deadlines. Customers with active deployments are also notified in advance, which is what makes this planning tractable.

distractorNotes.a: Retirement is a hard cutoff rather than a throttle. Requests to a retired model fail outright, so there is no degraded window to coast through.
distractorNotes.d: Identifiers do not repoint to a successor. Where an alias exists at all it resolves to a specific snapshot of the same model, never to a different replacement model, and silent substitution would change behavior untested.
distractorNotes.e: Customers running affected deployments receive advance notice of a retirement, and that notice period is exactly what makes an orderly migration plan possible.

sourceNote: Model deprecations - 'Migrating to replacements', 'Notifications', 'Auditing model usage', and 'Best practices' sections, plus the note that partner-operated platforms set their own retirement schedules

stem: A stakeholder asks only that the assistant should give good answers to billing questions. The team must turn that into a usable success criterion. Which restatement best satisfies the documented properties of being specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant?

options.text: On a held-out set of 2,000 labeled billing tickets, resolve at least 90 percent without escalation, above the measured baseline.
Answer billing questions accurately and helpfully in the large majority of the cases that customers actually raise in practice.
Outperform every competing product on all billing tasks by a margin that stakeholders agree is clearly wide enough to matter.
Never produce an incorrect billing answer under any input at all, including inputs that are adversarial or badly malformed.

explanation: Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant. The strong restatement names the exact behavior being judged, attaches a number to it, evaluates it on a held-out set of a stated size so the result generalizes rather than reflecting memorized examples, and anchors the target to a measured baseline so the goal is grounded in demonstrated performance rather than invented. The weak versions each fail on a different axis, which is what makes comparing them instructive. Note also that most real applications need several such criteria at once, spanning dimensions such as task fidelity, latency, and cost, since optimizing a single number in isolation usually degrades another.

distractorNotes.b: This restates the original vague request in slightly more words. Neither accurate, helpful, nor large majority is defined, so no one can determine whether the criterion has been met.
distractorNotes.c: This is neither measurable nor achievable as written. All billing tasks is unbounded, the margin is defined only by agreement, and competitor performance cannot be measured reliably.
distractorNotes.d: A demand for perfection under any input is not achievable and gives the team no usable target, since the criterion fails on the first edge case regardless of overall quality.

sourceNote: Define success criteria and build evaluations - 'Define your success criteria' section on specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant criteria, with its good-versus-bad criteria comparisons

stem: A team is building an evaluation suite for a Claude-based feature before it ships. Which practices match the documented evaluation design principles? Select THREE.

options.text: Build test cases that mirror the real task distribution, deliberately including edge cases rather than only representative ones.
Keep the suite small and exclusively human-graded, on the basis that human judgment is the only trustworthy signal available.
Structure cases so grading can be automated, for example through exact match, code-based checks, or model-based grading.
Favor a larger volume of automatically graded cases over a small hand-graded set, even when per-case signal is somewhat weaker.
Exclude ambiguous and adversarial inputs from the suite so that the resulting scores stay straightforward to interpret.
Reduce the suite to a single aggregate metric, since multidimensional criteria make results harder to compare across runs.

explanation: Three principles govern evaluation design. Evaluations should be task-specific, mirroring the distribution of work the system will actually face and deliberately including edge cases such as irrelevant or missing input, excessively long input, hostile user input, and cases ambiguous enough that human graders would themselves disagree. Grading should be automated wherever the question can be structured to allow it. Most counterintuitively, volume should be prioritized over per-case quality: a larger automatically graded set beats a smaller hand-graded one even though each individual case carries slightly less signal, because the aggregate is more informative and, critically, can be re-run cheaply on every change. That last property is what turns an evaluation suite into a regression gate rather than a one-off study.

distractorNotes.b: This inverts the stated priority. Hand-graded suites are too small and too slow to re-run, so they cannot serve as an ongoing regression signal.
distractorNotes.e: Ambiguous and adversarial inputs are named as edge cases worth including. Excluding them produces a comfortable score that says nothing about behavior where failure is most likely.
distractorNotes.f: Most use cases require multidimensional evaluation across several criteria. Collapsing to one number hides trade-offs, such as accuracy gains bought with unacceptable latency or cost.

sourceNote: Define success criteria and build evaluations - 'Build evaluations' section, 'Eval design principles' list covering task specificity, automation, and prioritizing volume over quality

stem: A team is prototyping a high-volume, latency-sensitive classification feature and has not yet established a quality bar for it. They want to follow the path that Anthropic's model-selection guidance labels as starting efficiency-first. Which sequence matches that path?

options.text: Implement with the strongest available model first, tune the prompts for it, then work toward more efficient models as the workflow matures.
Route production traffic to every available model in parallel for a week, then keep whichever one draws the fewest complaints from users.
Choose whichever model exposes the largest context window, on the basis that more available context reliably raises accuracy on any workload and leaves room to grow.
Implement with a faster, lower-cost model, test the use case thoroughly, evaluate against requirements, and upgrade only for a specific capability gap.

explanation: The efficiency-first path is a four-step loop: begin implementation with a faster, more cost-effective model, test the use case thoroughly, evaluate whether performance meets your requirements, and upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps. It is named as the better opening move for initial prototyping, applications with tight latency requirements, cost-sensitive implementations, and high-volume straightforward tasks, all of which describe this team. It also allows quick iteration and lower development costs while the quality bar is still being discovered.

distractorNotes.a: This is the capability-first path, the documented alternative rather than the one the question asks about. It is recommended for complex reasoning, scientific or mathematical work, nuanced understanding, and cases where accuracy outweighs cost.
distractorNotes.b: The documented way to choose between models is to create benchmark tests specific to the use case and compare candidates on accuracy, response quality, and edge-case handling. A production shootout scored by complaint volume is neither documented starting approach.
distractorNotes.c: Context window size is not a proxy for accuracy. The guidance states that more context is not automatically better, because accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, which makes curating what sits in context as important as how much room exists.

sourceNote: Choosing the right model - 'Choose the best model to start with', Option 1: Start efficiency-first (contrasted with Option 2: Start capability-first) and 'Decide whether to upgrade or change models'

stem: An existing integration comfortably meets its latency budget but is failing quality checks on inputs that need multi-step reasoning. The team's first instinct is to jump to a more capable model tier. What does Anthropic's model-selection guidance advise instead?

options.text: Raise max_tokens substantially, since shortfalls on multi-step reasoning are nearly always caused by responses being truncated before completion.
Build an evaluation set for the use case, compare candidates on accuracy, quality, and edge cases, and try raising effort before changing models at all.
Disable prompt caching while evaluating, since serving a prefix from cache alters the text the model generates and would therefore skew the comparison.
Move up a model tier immediately, since the effort parameter shifts only response latency and has no bearing whatsoever on reasoning quality.

explanation: Two pieces of guidance combine. Deciding whether to upgrade or change models begins with creating benchmark tests specific to the use case; having a good evaluation set is called the most important step in the process, followed by testing with actual prompts and data and comparing accuracy, response quality, and edge-case handling. Separately, effort appears among the key selection criteria with the explicit note that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models, because it trades intelligence against latency and cost inside a single model. With latency not the binding constraint here, raising effort is the cheaper experiment to run first.

distractorNotes.a: max_tokens is a hard ceiling on total output covering thinking plus response text. Exhausting it surfaces as a max_tokens stop reason and visibly cut-off text, a different symptom from answers that terminate normally but reason poorly.
distractorNotes.c: Prompt caching has no effect on output token generation; the response received is identical to what would be returned without caching. Disabling it during an evaluation removes a cost saving without improving the fidelity of the comparison.
distractorNotes.d: Effort is not a latency-only control. It governs how many tokens the model spends across the entire response, including thinking and tool calls, so it is a direct lever on reasoning depth rather than a neutral speed dial.

sourceNote: Choosing the right model - 'Establish key criteria' (Effort: tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models) and 'Decide whether to upgrade or change models'

stem: A developer is adopting the effort parameter to trade response thoroughness against token efficiency within a single model. Which THREE statements about how the effort parameter behaves are accurate? Select THREE.

options.text: It acts as a hard cap on output tokens, and generation is truncated as soon as the allowance attached to the selected level has been spent.
It applies to all output tokens, including tool calls and their arguments, rather than only to thinking content.
Passing the value that names the adaptive thinking mode is how you let the model choose its own effort level.
It has no effect on a request at all unless thinking has been explicitly enabled for that request.
Setting it explicitly to the model's default level behaves identically to omitting the parameter from the request.
It is a behavioral signal rather than a strict budget: at lower levels the model still reasons on hard problems, just less.

explanation: Effort controls how many tokens the model spends on a response, and it affects every output token: text and explanations, tool calls and their arguments, and thinking when it is active. That is why lower levels combine operations into fewer and terser tool calls and skip preamble. Explicitly setting the level that is already the default is documented as producing exactly the same behavior as omitting the parameter. And effort is described as a behavioral signal rather than a strict token budget, so at lower levels the model still thinks on sufficiently difficult problems, merely less than it would at a higher level for the same problem.

distractorNotes.a: The hard limit on total output, spanning thinking plus response text together, is max_tokens. Effort steers how much the model elects to spend and does not terminate generation once some allowance is reached.
distractorNotes.c: The adaptive value names a thinking mode, not an effort level, and the documentation explicitly warns against passing it as an effort value. Thinking mode and effort are separate controls that interact rather than substitute for one another.
distractorNotes.d: Because effort applies to every output token, it works whether or not thinking is enabled. Even with thinking inactive, a lower level still shortens explanations and reduces the number of tool calls made.

sourceNote: Effort - 'How effort works' (affects all tokens; setting the default is the same as omitting), 'Effort levels' (behavioral signal, not a strict token budget), and 'Effort with tool use'

stem: A service puts a large, unchanging instruction set in its leading content blocks, then appends one final block holding the current timestamp plus the incoming user message, and marks that final block with cache_control. Every response reports a non-zero cache creation count and a cache read count of zero. What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: Writes happen only at the breakpoint and the marked block differs each request, so the prefix hash never matches; move the breakpoint to the last unchanging block.
The backward lookback should find the stable prefix sitting behind the breakpoint, so entries must be expiring before reuse; switching to the longer cache duration will fix it.
The request exceeded the maximum number of cache breakpoints, so the surplus writes were silently discarded and only the earliest one was retained.
Read counts begin to populate only after a second successful write at the same position, so the cache is healthy and reads will appear on later turns.

explanation: Marking a block with cache_control writes exactly one entry: a hash of the entire prefix up to and including that block. Because the hash is cumulative, changing any block at or before the breakpoint produces a different hash on the next request. A timestamp and the incoming message change every time, so each request pays for a fresh write and never earns a read, which is worse than not caching at all. The documented remedy is to place cache_control on the last block whose prefix is identical across the requests meant to share a cache, here the end of the static instruction set, and keep the varying text after it. This prompt shape is also the case where automatic caching falls into the same trap, since it targets the last cacheable block.

distractorNotes.b: The lookback searches for entries earlier requests actually wrote, not for stable content sitting behind the breakpoint. Since no write ever occurred at those earlier positions, no duration setting helps; a longer lifetime only extends entries that already exist.
distractorNotes.c: Only one breakpoint is in play here, well under the limit of four, and breakpoints add no cost of their own. Supplying too many breakpoints surfaces as an error rather than as writes being quietly dropped.
distractorNotes.d: A matching prefix is reported as a read on the very next request that reuses it. A read count that stays at zero across many requests is the documented signal that no matching entry exists, not evidence of a warm-up period.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'Structuring your prompt' > 'How automatic prefix checking works' (Common mistake: Breakpoint on content that changes every request), 'Understanding cache breakpoint costs', and 'Best practices for effective caching'

stem: An agent harness appends many content blocks per turn and sets one cache_control breakpoint on the final block of each request. Early turns read from cache as expected, but deeper into a session the read count falls to zero even though the earlier conversation content never changes. What is the documented cause and remedy?

options.text: Every block in a run of consecutive tool_use blocks consumes a lookback position, so parallel tool calls are the cause and must be serialized.
Automatic caching removes the lookback limit entirely, because the system then takes over breakpoint placement on the developer's behalf.
The lookback spans a limited number of positions, so a turn can push the breakpoint past the previous entry; add a second, earlier breakpoint from the start.
Cache entries are evicted once the accumulated prompt nears the model's context window, so a compaction step has to run before cache reads can resume on subsequent turns.

explanation: On each request the system hashes the prefix at the breakpoint and, finding no match, walks backward one position at a time looking for an entry a prior request wrote. That search covers at most 20 positions per breakpoint, counting the breakpoint itself as the first. A conversation growing by many blocks per turn can push the current breakpoint 20 or more positions past the previous write, so the window misses it and the request pays a full write with no read. Because the lookback can only find entries earlier requests already wrote, the documented fix is to add a second breakpoint nearer that position from the outset, so a write accumulates there before it is needed. Up to four breakpoints are available and they add no cost of their own.

distractorNotes.a: A run of consecutive tool_use blocks counts as a single position, and so does a run of consecutive tool_result blocks. That rule exists precisely so that a turn with many parallel tool calls does not push the previous entry out of the window by itself.
distractorNotes.b: Automatic caching uses the same underlying infrastructure, so the same lookback window, minimum token thresholds, and prefix ordering rules still apply. It also consumes one of the four breakpoint slots rather than removing any limit.
distractorNotes.d: Entries lapse on their lifetime, not on prompt size, and cached prefixes still occupy the context window. Caching and context management address different problems, so compaction is not a prerequisite for getting a cache hit.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'How automatic prefix checking works' (three core principles; the 20-block lookback window; the growing-conversation example), 'When to use multiple breakpoints', and 'Automatic caching' > 'What stays the same'

stem: A cached request returns usage showing 100,000 cache read input tokens, 0 cache creation input tokens, and 50 input tokens. How should these three fields be interpreted?

options.text: 100,050 input tokens were processed; the plain input field covers only tokens after the last breakpoint, and all three categories occupy the window.
100,050 input tokens were processed, but the cached portion no longer counts against the context window, because it was billed at the discounted cache read rate instead.
Only 50 input tokens were processed, because cached content is retained server-side and is neither resent nor counted again on this request.
Exactly 100,000 input tokens were processed, because the plain input field is a subset of the cache read field rather than an addition to it.

explanation: The three fields are disjoint and sum to the total input processed, so 100,000 plus 0 plus 50 gives 100,050 tokens. The commonly misread field is the plain input token count, which represents only the content falling after the last cache breakpoint rather than the whole input, which is why it looks so small on a well-cached request. The split matters for cost attribution and for rate limits. It does not change context accounting: cached prefixes still occupy the context window, because caching changes what you pay for those tokens rather than whether they count.

distractorNotes.b: Cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window. The documentation is explicit that prompt caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count against the window's capacity.
distractorNotes.c: Caching changes what is charged for a matched prefix, not whether the prefix is transmitted. The full prompt is still sent on every request and still consumes context window capacity; only the price of the matched portion changes.
distractorNotes.d: The fields do not overlap. The plain input token count covers content after the last breakpoint, so it is additive to the cache read figure rather than a subset drawn from it.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'Tracking cache performance' > 'Understanding the token breakdown' (total input equals cache reads plus cache creation plus input_tokens); context accounting corroborated by Context windows - 'How the context window works'

stem: A team is choosing between the default cache lifetime and the extended cache lifetime for an assistant where a human user sometimes pauses between turns. Which TWO statements about how the two lifetimes behave are accurate? Select TWO.

options.text: The extended lifetime also lowers time to first token relative to the default lifetime, whether or not a given request actually turns out to hit the cache at all.
When most pauses run well past the extended lifetime, the extended option is still cheaper because it tolerates the longer gaps.
Its write costs twice the base input rate against 1.25 times for the default, so it needs roughly two reads to break even versus roughly one.
Reuse refreshes the default lifetime free of charge, and lifetime is measured from the start of the request rather than the end of its response.
Tokens served from cache are deducted against rate limits at the same weight as ordinary uncached input tokens would be.

explanation: The two lifetimes differ only in write price and duration. A write for the default lifetime carries a 1.25x multiplier on the base input rate and the extended lifetime carries a 2x multiplier, while a read is charged at a small fraction of the base input rate under either. That produces the documented break-even rule: caching pays off after roughly one read on the default duration and roughly two on the extended one. Operationally, the default lifetime is refreshed at no additional cost each time cached content is used, and the clock starts at the beginning of the request that writes or reads the entry rather than when its response finishes, so time spent generating counts against the remaining window.

distractorNotes.a: The two durations behave the same with respect to latency. An improvement in time to first token comes from getting a cache hit at all, which is most visible on long documents, and is not a property of the longer duration.
distractorNotes.b: A gap longer than the extended lifetime expires entries under either setting, and the extended option then rewrites the prefix at its higher write price, losing on each such gap. The guidance is to stay on the default when very long gaps dominate.
distractorNotes.e: Cache hits are not deducted against rate limits. Improved rate limit utilization is in fact listed as one of the documented reasons to reach for the extended duration in the first place.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'Pricing' (5-minute writes at 1.25x and 1-hour writes at 2x base input; reads at a fraction of it), 'How prompt caching works' (free refresh; lifetime measured from request start), and '1-hour cache duration' > 'When to use the 1-hour cache'

stem: Cache prefixes are created in a fixed order, tool definitions then the system prompt then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and every level after it. Which THREE statements about cache invalidation are accurate? Select THREE.

options.text: Passing the effort value the model already uses by default, instead of omitting the parameter, invalidates the cached prefix.
Additional cache breakpoints raise cost per request, so consolidating to a single breakpoint is the usual cure for a falling hit rate.
Editing a tool definition's name, description, or parameters invalidates the whole cache, system and message portions included.
Toggling a capability that rewrites the system prompt, such as web search or citations, keeps the tools portion but invalidates the rest.
Changing the tool choice setting, or adding or removing an image anywhere, invalidates messages while leaving tools and system valid.
Reordering the keys inside a tool use block's JSON is harmless, because the request is normalized before the prefix gets hashed.

explanation: Because tool definitions sit first in the prefix, any edit to their names, descriptions, or parameters invalidates everything downstream. Toggles that rewrite the system prompt, such as enabling or disabling web search or citations, sit one level lower: the tools cache stays valid while system and message caches are invalidated. Changes confined to the message level, including tool_choice and the presence or absence of images anywhere in the prompt, invalidate only message blocks. Reasoning down the tools, system, messages hierarchy is the reliable way to predict the blast radius of any given change before you ship it.

distractorNotes.a: Setting effort explicitly to the model's default is documented as equivalent to omitting it and does not invalidate. Changing effort to a different value does invalidate message blocks, and on some models the tools and system caches ahead of them as well.
distractorNotes.b: Breakpoints carry no cost of their own; charges accrue only for cache writes, cache reads, and uncached input. Consolidating to one breakpoint also inverts the guidance for a falling hit rate, where adding a breakpoint is what restores hits.
distractorNotes.f: Cache hits require byte-identical prompt segments, and a specific troubleshooting step warns that some languages randomize key order during JSON conversion, breaking caches. Stable key ordering in tool_use blocks has to be verified, not assumed.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'What invalidates the cache' (invalidation table covering tool definitions, web search and citations toggles, tool choice, images, and the effort setting), 'Understanding cache breakpoint costs', and 'Troubleshooting common issues'

stem: A developer marks a fairly short system prompt with cache_control. The requests succeed and no error is returned, but both the cache creation and cache read token counts are zero on every call. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the developer do about it?

options.text: cache_control is honored on a system block only when tool definitions are also present, so a tool definition has to be added to activate it.
The minimum cacheable length is identical on every model, so length cannot be the issue and the prompt must instead be failing exact matching.
Caching below the minimum is rejected with a validation error, so the zeroes point to a client bug that is dropping the cache_control field.
The content sits below the model's minimum cacheable length, which varies by model; caching is skipped silently, so check that model's threshold.

explanation: Prompts shorter than the minimum cacheable length for the model in use cannot be cached even when marked with cache_control. Crucially, such requests are processed without caching and no error is returned, which makes this a silent failure. The documented way to detect it is precisely the symptom described: both the cache creation and cache read token counts sitting at zero. Because the threshold differs by model, it must be looked up for the model actually being called. When a prompt falls just short, expanding the cached content to reach the threshold is often worthwhile, since reads cost significantly less than uncached input for frequently reused prompts.

distractorNotes.a: System content blocks are cacheable on their own. The tools array is simply an earlier position in the prefix hierarchy, not a precondition for caching anything that appears later in the prompt.
distractorNotes.b: The minimum differs by model, and partner-operated cloud platforms document their own per-model minimums, failure behavior, and usage field names. Assuming one universal threshold is a common source of exactly this bug.
distractorNotes.c: Caching below the minimum fails silently rather than raising an error. That is exactly why the response usage fields are documented as the way to confirm whether a prompt was actually cached at all.

sourceNote: Prompt caching - 'Caching strategies and considerations' > 'Cache limitations' (per-model minimum cacheable prompt length; requests below it are processed without caching and no error is returned; verify via the response usage fields)

stem: A team is moving a nightly evaluation workload onto the Message Batches API. Which THREE statements about batch processing are accurate? Select THREE.

options.text: Setting the streaming flag on a batched request delivers that request's output incrementally as the model produces it.
Prompt caching is disabled within a batch, so cache_control markers are ignored on every request submitted inside one.
Batch usage is charged at half the standard input and output rates, and that discount stacks with the prompt caching multipliers.
Each request's parameters are validated synchronously at submission, so a malformed request is rejected before the batch is created.
A batch expires if processing has not finished within 24 hours, and expired, canceled, and errored requests are not billed.
Results can be returned in any order, so each one must be reconciled using the unique identifier supplied with its request.

explanation: Batching trades latency for a 50 percent discount charged on both input and output tokens, and prompt caching multipliers stack with that discount rather than being excluded by it. The asynchronous contract carries two consequences worth internalizing: a batch expires if processing has not completed within 24 hours, and requests ending as expired, canceled, or errored are not billed, so failures carry no cost risk. Results also come with no ordering guarantee, which is why every request must carry a unique custom identifier and results must be reconciled by that identifier rather than by position in the submitted list.

distractorNotes.a: Streaming is one of the parameters explicitly unsupported inside a batch and returns a validation error, because batch results come back as a single results file rather than as a stream of per-request events.
distractorNotes.b: Caching works inside batches. The documented recommendation is in fact to consider the extended cache duration for batches that share context, precisely because a batch can take longer to process than the default cache lifetime.
distractorNotes.d: Validation of the parameters object for each request is performed asynchronously, and validation errors are returned only once processing of the entire batch has ended. This is why request shape should be verified against the synchronous Messages API first.

sourceNote: Batch processing - 'Batch limitations' (24-hour expiration), 'What can be batched' (unsupported parameters table including stream) plus its 1-hour cache tip, 'Pricing' (50% of standard rates), and 'Retrieving batch results' (result types and unbilled outcomes; results may not match input order)

stem: A team sized its prompts using figures from the token counting endpoint captured some time ago against an older model generation, then reused those stored figures when moving the workload to a newer generation. Requests now consume more input than budgeted. Which statement best explains the situation?

options.text: The endpoint rejects tool definitions, images, and PDFs, so any prompt containing them was undercounted by design from the outset.
The endpoint returns an exact, billable count that is identical on every model, so the overage must originate entirely from output tokens.
Counts are not portable across model generations, since a newer tokenizer yields more tokens for the same text; recount against the target model.
Counts include tokens that the platform adds for its own system optimizations, and those added tokens are billed to the caller, which is what explains the overage.

explanation: Two properties of token counting explain this. First, tokenization is a property of the model generation: a newer tokenizer produces more tokens for the same input text, with the exact increase depending on the content and workload shape, and the documentation therefore instructs recounting prompts against the model you plan to use rather than reusing counts measured against earlier models. Second, the returned figure is explicitly an estimate, and the actual number of input tokens used when creating a message may differ by a small amount. Together these make stale cross-generation counts an unreliable basis for budgeting, rate limit planning, or routing decisions.

distractorNotes.a: The endpoint accepts the same structured inputs used to create a message, including system prompts, tool definitions, images, and PDFs. One narrower nuance does apply: server tool token counts reflect only the first sampling call.
distractorNotes.b: The count is documented as an estimate rather than an exact billed figure, and a tokenizer change between generations shifts the count for identical text. Neither the model-independence nor the exactness claimed here holds.
distractorNotes.d: Counts may include tokens added automatically for system optimizations, but the documentation states you are not billed for system-added tokens and that billing reflects only your content, so they cannot explain a genuine cost overage.

sourceNote: Token counting - 'How to count message tokens' (the count is an estimate; system-added tokens are not billed) and 'Supported models' (newer tokenizer produces more tokens for the same input text; recount against the model you plan to use)

stem: Spend on a user-facing production agent loop is climbing as sessions run longer, while output quality remains acceptable. Anthropic's cost guidance separates levers that cut spend without touching quality from levers that trade quality for cost. Which action should the team take first, and why?

options.text: Move the loop onto the Batch API, because its discount is the single largest cost lever available on any workload whatsoever.
Turn on prompt caching, because each turn resends the whole growing conversation, making it the largest lever that costs no quality.
Enable the higher-throughput output mode, because producing tokens faster reduces the number of tokens billed for each session.
Lower the effort level, because cutting spend always requires surrendering capability and effort is the cleanest way to trade it away.

explanation: Caching is placed first among the levers that cut spend without touching quality, and the reasoning is structural: an agentic loop resends its system prompt, tool definitions, and every prior turn on each new turn, so task cost grows with roughly the square of the turn count. Caching does not stop the resending, but a matched prefix is billed at a fraction of the input rate and processes faster, and it is identified as the largest single lever by a wide margin. Because it costs nothing in quality, it should be exhausted before reaching for the levers that trade capability for cost.

distractorNotes.a: Batching is genuinely a free win, but only for work nobody is waiting on, since it trades latency for its discount and results may take up to 24 hours. A user-facing interactive loop cannot be routed through it, and caching is identified as the larger lever regardless.
distractorNotes.c: The higher-throughput output mode is a latency feature offered at premium rates over standard pricing. It changes how quickly tokens are produced, not how many are billed, so adopting it increases spend rather than reducing it.
distractorNotes.d: Effort is a real lever, but it belongs to the group that trades intelligence for cost rather than the group that cuts spend for free. The guidance is to take the levers carrying no quality cost first, then move along the cost-to-intelligence frontier.

sourceNote: Optimizing for cost and intelligence - 'Start here' (free wins versus tradeoffs) and 'Cut spend without losing quality' > 'Cache repeated context' > 'Why caching comes first'

stem: A developer runs a task with the Claude Agent SDK and sets no turn limit and no budget limit. Assuming the task completes normally, what causes the agent loop to stop so the SDK can emit its final result message?

options.text: Claude produces a response that contains no tool calls.
The accumulated conversation reaches the context window limit.
Every tool the agent was permitted to use has been called at least once.
The SDK reaches its default maximum number of turns.

explanation: The loop repeats one cycle: Claude evaluates the current state and may respond with text, tool calls, or both; the SDK executes any requested tools and feeds the results back for the next decision. That cycle continues until Claude answers without requesting any tools. At that point the SDK yields a final assistant message carrying the text, followed by a result message with the final text, token usage, cost, and session ID. Termination is therefore a property of the model's own output rather than of an external counter or a resource ceiling.

distractorNotes.b: Approaching the context limit triggers automatic compaction rather than termination. The SDK summarizes older history to free space, signals this with a system message marking a compaction boundary, and the loop continues.
distractorNotes.c: Nothing in the loop requires exhausting the available tool set. Claude selects tools based on the task, and many tasks finish having used only one or two of the tools offered to them.
distractorNotes.d: There is no default turn ceiling; the maximum-turns option applies only when you configure it. Even then, reaching it is an error termination reported through a dedicated error subtype, not the normal end of a completed task.

sourceNote: Sections 'The loop at a glance' and 'Turns and messages'

stem: A team is moving an Agent SDK agent into production and wants predictable ceilings on open-ended runs. Select TWO statements that accurately describe how the SDK's turn and budget limits behave.

options.text: The maximum-turns option counts tool-use turns only.
The maximum-turns option counts each individual tool call, so a turn requesting three tools consumes three of the allowance.
Spending by subagents counts toward the run's budget cap, and a run that stops there ends with a dedicated maximum-budget error subtype.
Subagent requests are metered separately from the parent run and are excluded from the budget cap.
When a run stops at the maximum-turns limit, the result message still carries the partial text the agent produced in its result field.

explanation: Both limits are fields on the options you pass when starting a run, and both default to no limit. The turn cap counts round trips in which Claude requested tools; the final text-only response that ends a task is not one of them. The budget cap is compared against the run's total cost, which aggregates every request the run made, including requests made by subagents it spawned. When either ceiling is reached the loop ends with a result message whose subtype names the limit that stopped it, which lets your code tell a completed task from a truncated one and, where appropriate, resume with a higher ceiling.

distractorNotes.b: The unit is the turn, not the tool call. A single turn can request several tools; the SDK executes them and feeds all the results back as one round trip, which consumes one turn.
distractorNotes.d: Subagents are not metered outside the run. Each subagent issues its own API requests, and those requests count toward the same total cost the budget cap is compared against, which is exactly why the cap is useful for bounding a run that fans out.
distractorNotes.e: The result text is available on a successful completion. On a run that ends at a limit, the subtype reports which limit was hit and no final result text is available, so code that reads the result field unconditionally will find nothing there.

sourceNote: Sections 'Control how the loop runs' subsection 'Turns and budget', and 'Handle the result'

stem: An Agent SDK agent is given a formatting rule in its opening prompt. It follows the rule early on, but many turns into the same long session it quietly stops applying it, even though no options or prompts were changed. What explains this, and what is the documented way to make the rule stick?

options.text: The context window is cleared between turns once a session grows long, so any instruction has to be repeated in each new prompt the application sends rather than being stated once at the start of the session.

The SDK lowers the reasoning effort level automatically as a session lengthens, and the rule will be honoured again once effort is raised back to the value the session started with, without any change to the prompt.

Automatic compaction replaced older history with a summary that dropped the rule; durable instructions belong in a project CLAUDE.md loaded through setting sources, since that content is supplied on every request.
